lesson.child_mission: Conductors allow electric current to pass easily (many metals); insulators resist current (plastic, rubber, dry wood) and are used for safety coverings.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Sort: aluminium foil; plastic ruler; steel staple; paper. Likely conductors vs insulators in a simple circuit test.

FEEDBACK
Foil and staple conduct; plastic and paper typically insulate (dry).

WATCH FOR
Testing with wet hands or mains electricity is dangerous — only use low-voltage kits.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Predict conductor/insulator for ten materials, then test in a kit circuit. Update a table with evidence. State one safety rule.

Write a short reflection naming one observation or step you corrected and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Conductors allow electric current to pass easily (many metals); insulators resist current (plastic, rubber, dry wood) and are used for safety coverings.
materials: Optional: safe everyday objects for observation

lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Predict conductor/insulator for ten materials, then test in a kit circuit. Update a table with evidence. State one safety rule. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Original response on new material: Foil and staple conduct; plastic and paper typically insulate (dry). Reasoning: I used conductor by attending to insulator rather than copying the worked model.

Parent: Written model 2: Common error: Testing with wet hands or mains electricity is dangerous — only use low-voltage kits. Correction: Foil and staple conduct; plastic and paper typically insulate (dry). Why: the correction restores accurate use of conductor.

Parent: Likely misconception: Testing with wet hands or mains electricity is dangerous — only use low-voltage kits. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Investigate or describe a fresh example (not the worked objects) that uses conductor. Record evidence and explain how it supports your claim.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one science misconception about conductor, correct it with evidence, and say why the correction works.

Parent: Marking notes: Require a new example, named observations and a claim–evidence link. / Require misconception + corrected claim + evidence reason..

Conductors allow electric current to pass easily (many metals); insulators resist current (plastic, rubber, dry wood) and are used for safety coverings.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.
